claim: The mammalian Y chromosome is critical for male sex determination and spermatogenesis.
source: The mammalian Y chromosome is critical for male sex determination and spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the entire review content and cited literature throughout the manuscript.

claim: Linking each Y gene to specific aspects of male reproduction has been challenging.
source: However, linking each Y gene to specific aspects of male reproduction has been challenging.
evidence: This statement reflects the historical difficulty in the field, supported by the discussion of experimental limitations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Y chromosome is notoriously hard to sequence and target.
source: As the Y chromosome is notoriously hard to sequence and target, functional studies have mostly relied on transgene-rescue approaches using mouse models with large multi-gene deletions.
evidence: This is supported by discussion of technical challenges and the repetitive nature of the Y chromosome throughout the manuscript.

claim: Functional studies of the Y chromosome have mostly relied on transgene-rescue approaches using mouse models with large multi-gene deletions.
source: As the Y chromosome is notoriously hard to sequence and target, functional studies have mostly relied on transgene-rescue approaches using mouse models with large multi-gene deletions.
evidence: This is supported by the detailed discussion of transgene rescue experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: In therian mammals, with some exceptions, whether an embryo will develop into a male or a female is defined by the presence or absence of a Y chromosome.
source: In therian mammals, with some exceptions, whether an embryo will develop into a male or a female is defined by the presence or absence of a Y chromosome (Capel, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Capel, 2017.

claim: Males bear an X and a Y chromosome, whereas females carry two X chromosomes.
source: Males bear an X and a Y, whereas females carry two X chromosomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mammalian sex chromosome composition.

claim: From the 1950s, the Y chromosome was considered to be a genetic wasteland as studies of human pedigrees were only uncovering traits with autosomal or X-linked inheritance.
source: From the 1950s, it was considered to be a genetic wasteland as studies of human pedigrees were only uncovering traits with autosomal or X-linked inheritance (Stern, 1957).
evidence: This historical perspective is supported by citation to Stern, 1957.

claim: In 1959, it was shown that the male-determining gene is Y-linked.
source: In 1959, it was shown that the male-determining gene is Y-linked, but this was considered an exception on an otherwise functionally inert chromosome (Ford et al., 1959; Jacobs and Strong, 1959).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ford et al., 1959 and Jacobs and Strong, 1959.

claim: When transcription units were first discovered on the Y chromosome, they were thought to be inactive vestiges of their former autosomal ancestors.
source: When transcription units were first discovered on the Y chromosome (Agulnik et al., 1994; Arnemann et al., 1991; Page et al., 1987; Reijo et al., 1995; Salido et al., 1992; Sinclair et al., 1990), they were thought to be inactive vestiges of their former autosomal ancestors (Marshall Graves, 1995).
evidence: This historical perspective is supported by multiple citations including Marshall Graves, 1995.

claim: The 'impending demise' theory hypothesised a continuous loss of Y-protein-coding genes predicting the eventual loss of the Y chromosome.
source: More recently, the 'impending demise' theory hypothesised a continuous loss of Y-protein-coding genes predicting the eventual loss of the Y chromosome (Aitken and Marshall Graves, 2002; Marshall Graves, 2004).
evidence: This theory is supported by citations to Aitken and Marshall Graves, 2002 and Marshall Graves, 2004.

claim: The view of the Y as a disappearing genetic desert is incorrect.
source: We now know that the view of the Y as a disappearing genetic desert is incorrect.
evidence: This is an inference based on decades of research discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: Besides controlling male gonadal sex determination, the Y chromosome is crucial for initialisation, maintenance, and completion of spermatogenesis.
source: Decades of research have proved that besides controlling male gonadal sex determination, the Y chromosome is crucial for initialisation, maintenance, and completion of spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive discussion of Y chromosome functions in spermatogenesis throughout the manuscript.

claim: The mammalian heteromorphic X and Y chromosomes have evolved from an ancestral pair of autosomes.
source: The mammalian heteromorphic X and Y chromosomes have evolved from an ancestral pair of autosomes (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1 and is a well-established concept in sex chromosome evolution.

claim: The concept that sex chromosomes evolved from autosomes was hypothesised by Ohno, 1967.
source: This seminal concept, like many principles governing sex chromosome evolution, was hypothesised by Ohno, 1967.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ohno, 1967.

claim: Breakthroughs in Y-chromosome sequencing and assembly have been crucial to understand sex-chromosome evolution.
source: Henceforth, breakthroughs in Y-chromosome sequencing and assembly, which were long hindered by the Y's repeat-rich nature and homology to the X chromosome, have been crucial to understand sex-chromosome evolution (Bellott et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Skaletsky et al., 2003; Soh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to sequencing studies.

claim: Divergence into a 'proto-Y' started following mutations of Sox3, creating the sex-determining region Sry gene.
source: We now know that divergence into a 'proto-Y' started following mutations of Sox3, creating the sex-determining region Sry gene (Foster and Graves, 1994; Marshall Graves, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Foster and Graves, 1994 and Marshall Graves, 1998.

claim: The evolution of Sry-specific sex determination is thought to have happened around 160–166 million years ago after the split between therians and monotremes.
source: The evolution of Sry-specific sex determination is thought to have happened around 160–166 million years ago after the split between therians and monotremes (egg-laying mammals) (Potrzebowski et al., 2008; Veyrunes et al., 2008), and prior to the split between marsupials (metatherians) and eutherians (Luo et al., 2011).
evidence: This timing is supported by citations to Potrzebowski et al., 2008; Veyrunes et al., 2008; and Luo et al., 2011.

claim: The male-specific inheritance of the proto-Y exposed it to unique evolutionary forces.
source: The male-specific inheritance of the proto-Y exposed it to unique evolutionary forces (Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Larson et al., 2018.

claim: Male-specific inheritance facilitated selection and accumulation of male-beneficial mutations in the vicinity of Sry.
source: Notably, it facilitated selection and accumulation of male-beneficial mutations in the vicinity of Sry (Figure 1).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and is based on evolutionary theory.

claim: The linkage between Sry and male-beneficial loci created selective pressure to supress X-Y crossing over.
source: The linkage between Sry and male-beneficial loci in turn created selective pressure to supress X-Y crossing over.
evidence: This is based on evolutionary theory of sex chromosome evolution.

claim: Multiple discrete inversions on the Y supported and amplified meiotic-recombination arrest in specific regions, or strata.
source: Eventually, multiple discrete inversions on the Y supported and amplified meiotic-recombination arrest in specific regions, or strata (Figure 1; Bellott et al., 2014; Cortez et al., 2014; Lahn and Page, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1 and citations to Bellott et al., 2014; Cortez et al., 2014; Lahn and Page, 1999.

claim: Stratification expanded the non-recombining male-specific region at the expense of the pseudoautosomal region (PAR).
source: Stratification expanded the non-recombining male-specific region at the expense of the recombining portion of the chromosome known as the pseudoautosomal region (PAR) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and is a consequence of the stratification process.

claim: (Retro)transpositions/translocations from autosomes have occurred more recently in various mammalian lineages.
source: In addition to these strata, (retro)transpositions/translocations from autosomes have occurred more recently in various mammalian lineages (Bellott et al., 2014; Cortez et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bellott et al., 2014; Cortez et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2012.

claim: The loss of recombination associated with stratification allowed accumulation of Y-linked loss-of-function mutations, triggering chromosome-wide gene decay and amplification of repetitive DNA.
source: Importantly, the loss of recombination associated with stratification allowed accumulation of Y-linked loss-of-function mutations, triggering chromosome-wide gene decay and amplification of repetitive DNA (Bachtrog, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bachtrog, 2013.

claim: Large deletions of deleterious and non-functional DNA regions occurred within each non-recombining stratum as a mechanism to maintain male fitness.
source: As a mechanism to maintain male fitness, large deletions of deleterious and non-functional DNA regions occurred within each non-recombining stratum (Bachtrog, 2013; Hughes and Page, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bachtrog, 2013 and Hughes and Page, 2015.

claim: 98% of the ancestral human X-genes survived.
source: Although 98% of the ancestral human X-genes survived (Mueller et al., 2013), only 3% persisted on the human Y (Bellott et al., 2014; Skaletsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mueller et al., 2013.

claim: Only 3% of ancestral genes persisted on the human Y.
source: Although 98% of the ancestral human X-genes survived (Mueller et al., 2013), only 3% persisted on the human Y (Bellott et al., 2014; Skaletsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bellott et al., 2014 and Skaletsky et al., 2003.

claim: Although the Y experienced rapid decay early in evolution, degeneration then dramatically slowed down, with genes having survived this 'purge' showing stability.
source: However, although the Y experienced rapid decay early in evolution, degeneration then dramatically slowed down, with genes having survived this 'purge' showing stability (Bellott et al., 2014; Cortez et al., 2014; Hughes et al., 2012; Hughes et al., 2010; Hughes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to evolutionary studies.

claim: Of the 18 ancestral genes present in the ~97 million year old eutherian ancestor, humans retain 14, bull 13, chimp 11, and mouse 9.
source: For instance, of the 18 ancestral genes present in the ~97 million year old eutherian ancestor (Bellott et al., 2014), humans retain 14, bull 13, chimp 11, and mouse 9.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellott et al., 2014 and represents comparative genomic data.

claim: In humans, no Y genes appear to have been lost in the last 44 million years.
source: In humans, no Y genes appear to have been lost in the last 44 million years.
evidence: This is an inference from comparative genomic studies discussed in the manuscript.

claim: One stratum independently evolved in both therian lineages (eutherians and marsupials).
source: In addition, the longevity of certain X-Y gene pairs has been convergent between eutherians and marsupials. Indeed, one stratum independently evolved in both therian lineages (Figure 1).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 1 and supported by evolutionary studies.

claim: Two genes on the independently evolved stratum have convergently survived, suggesting that Y gene decay is not stochastic.
source: Two genes on this stratum have convergently survived, suggesting that Y gene decay is not stochastic (Bellott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bellott et al., 2014 and represents an inference from comparative data.

claim: X-Y gene-pair retention did not occur at random.
source: Altogether, it is likely that X-Y gene-pair retention did not occur at random.
evidence: This is an inference based on the patterns of gene retention discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Two evolutionary strategies have protected a specific set of Y genes: maintenance of ancestral X-Y gene pairs which are sensitive to transcriptional dosage; or retention and amplification of testis-biased gene families.
source: Generally, it is thought that two evolutionary strategies have protected a specific set of Y genes: maintenance of ancestral X-Y gene pairs which are sensitive to transcriptional dosage; or retention and amplification of testis-biased gene families.
evidence: This is a synthesis of evolutionary theory discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: Twofold X-chromosome upregulation in both males and females re-established X:A equilibrium in males.
source: Firstly, twofold X-chromosome upregulation in both males and females re-established X:A equilibrium in males (Table 1; Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 and citation to Deng et al., 2014.

claim: X-chromosome inactivation is a process by which one X is transcriptionally silenced in females, bringing the overall X-output level to that of the autosomes.
source: This was prevented by the evolution of X-chromosome inactivation, a process by which one X is transcriptionally silenced in females, bringing the overall X-output level to that of the autosomes (Table 1; Brockdorff et al., 2020; Loda and Heard, 2019; Lyon, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by Table 1 and citations to Brockdorff et al., 2020; Loda and Heard, 2019; Lyon, 1961.

claim: Y ancestral genes that share ubiquitous housekeeping regulatory functions with their X homologue have preferentially survived on the Y.
source: For instance, studies indicate that Y ancestral genes that share ubiquitous housekeeping regulatory functions with their X homologue, which would be very sensitive to change in expression levels, have preferentially survived on the Y (Bellott et al., 2014; Cortez et al., 2014; Jegalian and Page, 1998; Lahn and Page, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to evolutionary studies.

claim: The annotations of remaining X-Y pairs link them to the sensitive regulation of histone lysine demethylation, stem-cell self-renewal, splicing, translation initiation and deubiquitylation.
source: Indeed, the annotations of remaining X-Y pairs link them to the sensitive regulation of histone lysine demethylation, stem-cell self-renewal, splicing, translation initiation and deubiquitylation (Bellott et al., 2014; Lahn and Page, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bellott et al., 2014 and Lahn and Page, 1997.

claim: A higher proportion of X-linked genes with a surviving Y homologue escape X-inactivation, compared to genes with no Y homologues or with those showing signs of functional differentiation.
source: Indeed, the study of allele-specific expression in human, mouse and opossum has revealed that a higher proportion of X-linked genes with a surviving Y homologue escape X-inactivation, compared to genes with no Y homologues or with those showing signs of functional differentiation (Bellott et al., 2014; Cortez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bellott et al., 2014 and Cortez et al., 2014.

claim: Human X monosomy is associated with poor embryonic viability and individuals surviving into adulthood tend to be mosaic for at least part of the second sex chromosome.
source: Indeed, human X monosomy is associated with poor embryonic viability and individuals surviving into adulthood tend to be mosaic for at least part of the second sex chromosome.
evidence: This is based on clinical knowledge of Turner syndrome.

claim: Turner syndrome is less severe in mice than in humans, even in fully XO animals.
source: Interestingly, Turner syndrome is less severe in mice, even in fully XO animals (Burgoyne et al., 1983b; Burgoyne et al., 1983a; Burgoyne and Baker, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burgoyne et al., 1983b; Burgoyne et al., 1983a; Burgoyne and Baker, 1981.

claim: Mice have fewer surviving Y-linked ancestral genes (9) compared to humans (17).
source: This could be in part because mice have fewer surviving Y-linked ancestral genes (9 vs 17 in humans) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 2 and represents comparative genomic data.

claim: Ancestral, single-copy genes have sometimes diverged towards male-specific reproductive functions.
source: Another strategy thought to have protected Y-genes from regulatory and structural decay is the specialisation towards functions in male fertility. Indeed, ancestral, single-copy genes have sometimes diverged towards male-specific reproductive functions.
evidence: This is based on evolutionary analysis discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The expression of some Y genes became almost exclusively limited to the testis, gradually losing expression in other organs to become testis-biased.
source: The expression of some Y genes became almost exclusively limited to the testis, gradually losing expression in other organs to become testis-biased (Jegalian and Page, 1998; Mitchell, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jegalian and Page, 1998 and Mitchell, 2000.

claim: The Y chromosome has gained additional testis-biased genes through (retro)transposition and translocation events from autosomes.
source: In parallel, the Y chromosome has gained additional testis-biased genes through (retro)transposition and translocation events from autosomes (Burgoyne, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burgoyne, 1998.

claim: Some recently acquired testis-biased X/Y gene homologues have been massively amplified, forming tandem and palindromic repeats.
source: Importantly, some recently acquired testis-biased X/Y gene homologues have been massively amplified, forming tandem and palindromic repeats (Hughes et al., 2020; Rozen et al., 2003; Skaletsky et al., 2003; Soh et al., 2014; Trombetta and Cruciani, 2017; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: Repeats have been maintained and homogenised through intra-chromosomal recombination.
source: Following amplification, repeats have been maintained and homogenised through intra-chromosomal recombination (Trombetta and Cruciani, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Trombetta and Cruciani, 2017.

claim: In mice, bull and likely other mammals, amplification of sex chromosomes is thought to have been driven by the presence of antagonistic meiotic drivers (selfish genes) on the X and Y, each competing for transmission to the next generation.
source: In mice, bull and likely other mammals, amplification of sex chromosomes is thought to have been driven by the presence of antagonistic meiotic drivers (selfish genes) on the X and Y, each competing for transmission to the next generation (Cocquet et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2011; Hughes et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cocquet et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2011; Hughes et al., 2020; Soh et al., 2014.

claim: Surviving mammalian Y genes tend to fall into two categories: testis-specialised fertility genes or dosage-sensitive ubiquitous housekeepers.
source: Altogether, evolutionary insights have shown that surviving mammalian Y genes tend to fall into two categories: testis-specialised fertility genes or dosage-sensitive ubiquitous housekeepers (Lahn and Page, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lahn and Page, 1997 and represents a synthesis of evolutionary insights.

claim: Spermatogenesis allows continuous formation of gametes from spermatogonial stem cells.
source: Spermatogenesis allows continuous formation of gametes from spermatogonial stem cells (Figure 3).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3 and is established biological knowledge.

claim: Spermatogenesis can broadly be divided in three phases: mitosis, meiosis and spermiogenesis.
source: It occurs in cycles and can broadly be divided in three phases: mitosis, meiosis and spermiogenesis (Figure 3).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3 and is established biological knowledge.

claim: In mouse, one spermatogenic cycle can be dissected into 12 stages occurring over 8.6 days.
source: In mouse, one cycle can be dissected into 12 stages occurring over 8.6 days, and four cycles (35 days) are required to complete spermatogenesis, from spermatogonial stem cells to mature spermatozoa (de Rooij, 2017; Oakberg, 1956a; Oakberg, 1956b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Rooij, 2017; Oakberg, 1956a; Oakberg, 1956b.

claim: Four cycles (35 days) are required to complete spermatogenesis in mouse, from spermatogonial stem cells to mature spermatozoa.
source: In mouse, one cycle can be dissected into 12 stages occurring over 8.6 days, and four cycles (35 days) are required to complete spermatogenesis, from spermatogonial stem cells to mature spermatozoa (de Rooij, 2017; Oakberg, 1956a; Oakberg, 1956b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to de Rooij, 2017; Oakberg, 1956a; Oakberg, 1956b.

claim: In humans, one spermatogenic cycle is completed every 16 days.
source: In humans, one spermatogenic cycle is completed every 16 days, and ~72 days are needed for full differentiation of spermatogonial stem cells into spermatozoa (Muciaccia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muciaccia et al., 2013.

claim: ~72 days are needed for full differentiation of spermatogonial stem cells into spermatozoa in humans.
source: In humans, one spermatogenic cycle is completed every 16 days, and ~72 days are needed for full differentiation of spermatogonial stem cells into spermatozoa (Muciaccia et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muciaccia et al., 2013.

claim: Primordial germ cells are specified at embryonic day (E) 6.25 in mouse and E12 in humans.
source: Early in embryogenesis, at embryonic day (E) 6.25 in mouse and E12 in humans, the primordial germ cells are specified and subsequently migrate to the genital ridge (Kurimoto and Saitou, 2019; Sybirna et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurimoto and Saitou, 2019; Sybirna et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2016.

claim: The early bipotent gonad is formed at E10.5–11.5 in mouse and week six in humans.
source: The early bipotent gonad is formed at E10.5–11.5 in mouse and week six in humans.
evidence: This is based on developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Sry triggers a signalling cascade resulting in the supporting cell lineage differentiating into Sertoli cells.
source: Sry then triggers a signalling cascade resulting in the supporting cell lineage differentiating into Sertoli cells (Capel, 2017; Kurimoto and Saitou, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Capel, 2017 and Kurimoto and Saitou, 2019.

claim: Germ cell proliferation occurs until developmental arrest at E13.5 in mouse and after week 20 in human.
source: Germ cell proliferation will then occur until developmental arrest at E13.5 in mouse and after week 20 in human (Kurimoto and Saitou, 2019; Tam and Snow, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kurimoto and Saitou, 2019 and Tam and Snow, 1981.

claim: After birth, at around postnatal day (P) three in mouse and 2 months in humans, germ cells resume cell division.
source: After birth, at around postnatal day (P) three in mouse and 2 months in humans, germ cells resume cell division, giving rise to undifferentiated spermatogonial cells that are found at the basal compartment of seminiferous tubules.
evidence: This is based on developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Male meiosis is initiated in a synchronous manner during puberty, at P10 in mouse and ~13 years in humans.
source: Male meiosis is initiated in a synchronous manner during puberty, at P10 in mouse and ~13 years in humans.
evidence: This is based on developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Prophase I takes 2 weeks in mouse.
source: Meiosis occurs through two rounds of cell division. During prophase I, which takes 2 weeks in mouse, diploid primary spermatocytes (2 N:4 C) enter leptonema, zygonema, pachynema, and diplonema successively (Figure 3; Baudat et al., 2013; Oakberg, 1956b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baudat et al., 2013 and Oakberg, 1956b.

claim: At leptonema, meiotic DNA double-strand breaks are formed.
source: At leptonema, meiotic DNA double-strand breaks are formed.
evidence: This is established knowledge of meiotic processes.

claim: At zygonema, homologous chromosomes synapse and form bivalents.
source: At zygonema, homologous chromosomes synapse and form bivalents (Figure 3).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 3 and is established knowledge of meiotic processes.

claim: The X and Y are transcriptionally silenced at pachynema through the process of meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI).
source: Unlike autosomes, the X and Y are transcriptionally silenced at pachynema through the process of meiotic sex chromosome inactivation (MSCI) (Turner, 2015) and compartmentalised into a specialised chromatin domain called the sex body (Figure 3; McKee and Handel, 1993; Solari, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Turner, 2015; McKee and Handel, 1993; Solari, 1974 and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: MSCI failure leads to pachytene arrest and apoptosis.
source: MSCI failure leads to pachytene arrest and apoptosis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of meiotic quality control.

claim: MSCI persists throughout diplonema, when homologous chromosomes start to separate.
source: MSCI persists throughout diplonema, when homologous chromosomes start to separate (Burgoyne et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burgoyne et al., 2009.

claim: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) ensures proper chromosome alignment and spindle attachment at metaphase I.
source: After prophase I, metaphase I takes place and chromosome homologues are lined up along the metaphase plate. At this stage, the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) ensures proper chromosome alignment and spindle attachment (Figure 3; Lane and Kauppi, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lane and Kauppi, 2019 and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Spermiogenesis is characterised by the emergence of unique sperm-specific morphological features and by dramatic epigenetic reprogramming.
source: Spermiogenesis is characterised by the emergence of unique sperm-specific morphological features and by dramatic epigenetic reprogramming (Bao and Bedford, 2016; O'Donnell, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bao and Bedford, 2016 and O'Donnell, 2014.

claim: DNA of differentiating spermatids undergo increasing compaction in the nucleus.
source: Importantly, DNA of differentiating spermatids undergo increasing compaction in the nucleus (O'Donnell, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Donnell, 2014.

claim: Near genome-wide replacement of histones with protamines occurs during spermiogenesis.
source: This is achieved notably through near genome-wide replacement of histones with protamines.
evidence: This is established knowledge of spermiogenesis.

claim: Protamines permit an up to 20-fold increase in chromatin condensation.
source: Protamines permit an up to 20-fold increase in chromatin condensation (Balhorn, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Balhorn, 2007.

claim: Most X/Y-linked genes remain repressed throughout spermiogenesis.
source: Interestingly, most X/Y-linked genes remain repressed throughout spermiogenesis (Greaves et al., 2006; Namekawa et al., 2006; Sin et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2006), but some are re-activated (Hendriksen, 1999; Hendriksen et al., 1995; Mueller et al., 2013; Mueller et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greaves et al., 2006; Namekawa et al., 2006; Sin et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2006.

claim: Some X/Y-linked genes are re-activated during spermiogenesis.
source: Interestingly, most X/Y-linked genes remain repressed throughout spermiogenesis (Greaves et al., 2006; Namekawa et al., 2006; Sin et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2006), but some are re-activated (Hendriksen, 1999; Hendriksen et al., 1995; Mueller et al., 2013; Mueller et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hendriksen, 1999; Hendriksen et al., 1995; Mueller et al., 2013; Mueller et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Studies of mice and humans with Turner (XO) or Klinefelter (XXY) syndrome showed that in eutherian mammals, sex was determined by the presence/absence of the Y, independent of the number of X chromosomes.
source: The first evidence of the Y chromosome having any biological function arose from studies of mice (Welshons and Russell, 1959) and humans with Turner (XO) or Klinefelter (XXY) syndrome (Ford et al., 1959; Jacobs and Strong, 1959). These reports showed that in eutherian mammals, sex was determined by the presence/absence of the Y, independent of the number of X chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Welshons and Russell, 1959; Ford et al., 1959; Jacobs and Strong, 1959.

claim: Research on sex-reversed men showed that these XX males carried translocated DNA from the Y chromosome on one of their X chromosome.
source: For instance, using DNA hybridisation with several Y-DNA probes, it was showed that these XX males carried translocated DNA from the Y chromosome on one of their X chromosome (Guellaen et al., 1984; Page, 1986; Page et al., 1987; Page et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guellaen et al., 1984; Page, 1986; Page et al., 1987; Page et al., 1985.

claim: The candidate region for the male-determining factor was narrowed to 35 kb containing SRY.
source: As additional XX males were studied and the number of markers increased, the candidate region was narrowed to 35 kb containing SRY (Sinclair et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sinclair et al., 1990.

claim: The mouse orthologue of SRY was cloned and found to be expressed in specific somatic cells of the embryonic gonad at the time of testis differentiation.
source: The mouse orthologue was cloned and found to be expressed in specific somatic cells of the embryonic gonad at the time of testis differentiation (Gubbay et al., 1990; Koopman et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gubbay et al., 1990 and Koopman et al., 1990.

claim: Both sex-reversed XY mice and women had mutations in Sry.
source: It was also shown that both sex-reversed XY mice and women had mutations in Sry (Berta et al., 1990; Jäger et al., 1990; Lovell-Badge and Robertson, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berta et al., 1990; Jäger et al., 1990; Lovell-Badge and Robertson, 1990.

claim: In mouse, Sry alone is sufficient to induce testicular development.
source: Finally, it was shown that, in mouse, Sry alone is sufficient to induce testicular development (Koopman et al., 1991), as XX mice transgenic for Sry developed as males.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Koopman et al., 1991.

claim: Sry is a transcription factor of the SOX family that encodes a protein with an high mobility group (HMG)-box DNA binding domain.
source: Sry is a transcription factor of the SOX family that encodes a protein with an high mobility group (HMG)-box DNA binding domain (Table 2; Kashimada and Koopman, 2010; Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kashimada and Koopman, 2010 and shown in Table 2 and Figure 2.

claim: During murine embryogenesis, Sry upregulates Sox9 in Sertoli cell precursors between E11.5 and E12.5.
source: During murine embryogenesis, Sry upregulates Sox9 in Sertoli cell precursors between E11.5 and E12.5 (Kashimada and Koopman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kashimada and Koopman, 2010.

claim: SOX9 activates fibroblast growth factor 9 (Fgf9) in a feedforward loop, which represses Wnt4 and the female pathway.
source: SOX9 then activates fibroblast growth factor 9 (Fgf9) in a feedforward loop, which represses Wnt4 and the female pathway that would otherwise trigger ovary development (Capel, 2017; Kashimada and Koopman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Capel, 2017 and Kashimada and Koopman, 2010.

claim: Minor alteration in amount and timing of Sry expression leads to sex-reversal phenotypes.
source: Indeed, minor alteration in amount and timing of Sry expression leads to sex-reversal phenotypes (Kashimada and Koopman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kashimada and Koopman, 2010.

claim: The first sign that the Y chromosome may be involved in gamete production after testis determination came from the study of sub/infertile men with de novo deletions on the Y.
source: In humans, the first sign that the Y chromosome may be involved in gamete production after testis determination came from the study of sub/infertile men with de novo deletions on the Y (Tiepolo and Zuffardi, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tiepolo and Zuffardi, 1976.

claim: Three recurrently deleted regions of the human Y long arm were encountered: AZFa, AZFb, and AZFc.
source: With an increasing number of studies finding sub-fertile males with Y deletions, and with the advances of physical and molecular mapping, three recurrently deleted regions of the human Y long arm were encountered: AZFa, AZFb, and AZFc (Vogt et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vogt et al., 1996.

claim: Classic gene targeting strategies based on homologous recombination in mouse embryonic stem cells proved to be unsuccessful for the Y chromosome.
source: However, classic gene targeting strategies based on homologous recombination in mouse embryonic stem cells, which had worked to study autosomal and X gene functions, proved to be unsuccessful for the Y chromosome.
evidence: This reflects the technical challenges discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Mice with one X chromosome and transgenic expression of Sry (XOSry) develop testis populated with pro-spermatogonia that fail to proliferate, leading to absence of meiotic and post-meiotic cells.
source: Mice with one X chromosome and transgenic expression of Sry (XOSry) develop testis populated with pro-spermatogonia that fail to proliferate, leading to absence of meiotic and post-meiotic cells (Figure 4; Mazeyrat et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mazeyrat et al., 2001 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: A similar phenotype to XOSry can be observed in XO germ cells within XO/XY/XYY male mosaic mice.
source: A similar phenotype can be observed in XO germ cells within XO/XY/XYY male mosaic mice (Levy and Burgoyne, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levy and Burgoyne, 1986.

claim: Additional Y genes are necessary not only in germ cells, but also in testicular somatic cells that are key to support successful spermatogenesis.
source: Furthermore, it seems that additional Y genes are necessary not only in germ cells, but also in testicular somatic cells that are key to support successful spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental evidence discussed.

claim: XY spermatogonia transplanted into XXSry testis cannot complete spermatogenesis, whereas segments of immature XY seminiferous tubule transplanted into XXSry testis display normal spermatogenic development of XY germ cells.
source: Indeed, XY spermatogonia transplanted into XXSry testis cannot complete spermatogenesis, whereas segments of immature XY seminiferous tubule transplanted into XXSry testis display normal spermatogenic development of XY germ cells (Ishii et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ishii et al., 2007.

claim: Mazeyrat and colleagues used BAC or cosmid clones of Y genes to generate individual transgenic mouse lines for three single-copy Y genes.
source: In 2001, Mazeyrat et al., 2001 used BAC or cosmid clones of Y genes to generate individual transgenic mouse lines for three single-copy Y genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mazeyrat et al., 2001.

claim: Eif2s3y is an ancestral gene that has been lost in humans but is ubiquitously expressed in mouse and encodes a subunit of the translation initiation factor Eif2.
source: This ancestral gene has been lost in humans but is ubiquitously expressed in mouse and encodes a subunit of the translation initiation factor Eif2 (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: Testes of mice expressing an Eif2s3y transgene were larger than XOSry controls.
source: Testes of these 'rescued' mice were larger than XOSry controls.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Mazeyrat et al., 2001.

claim: The proportion of spermatogonia in Eif2s3y-rescued mice was similar to that of wild types.
source: Furthermore, the proportion of spermatogonia in rescued mice was similar to that of wild types.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Mazeyrat et al., 2001.

claim: Germ cells in Eif2s3y-rescued mice progressed to the secondary spermatocyte stage, only arresting before the second meiotic division.
source: Importantly, germ cells progressed to the secondary spermatocyte stage, only arresting before the second meiotic division (Figure 4).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 4 and based on experimental results.

claim: Occasionally, spermatid-like cells were observed in Eif2s3y-rescued mouse models, although most of them were abnormally shaped and diploid.
source: Occasionally, spermatid-like cells were observed in these mouse models, although most of them were abnormally shaped and diploid (Figure 4; Mazeyrat et al., 2001; Vernet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mazeyrat et al., 2001 and Vernet et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Yamauchi and colleagues were able to fertilise donor oocytes by injecting the rare round spermatids found in the testis of Sry and Eif2s3y-complemented mouse models.
source: Using assisted reproduction, they were able to fertilise donor oocytes by injecting the rare round spermatids found in the testis of Sry and Eif2s3y-complemented mouse models.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Yamauchi et al., 2014.

claim: In mice expressing an additional fragment of the Y chromosome short arm, the abundance of later stage spermatids and the success of assisted reproduction was increased.
source: For instance, Yamauchi and colleagues showed that in mice expressing an additional fragment of the Y chromosome short arm, the abundance of later stage spermatids and the success of assisted reproduction was increased.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results from Yamauchi et al., 2014.

claim: The zinc-finger Y-linked Zfy1 and Zfy2 are a family of duplicated paralogues.
source: In particular, a family of duplicated paralogues, the zinc-finger Y-linked Zfy1 and Zfy2 (Figure 2 and Table 2), has received much attention in the last decade and has been described as a key regulator of multiple spermatogenesis events.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: The Zfy transcription factors are conserved across eutherians.
source: The Zfy transcription factors are conserved across eutherians (Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: In humans, the single ZFY has two splice variants.
source: In humans, the single ZFY has two splice variants.
evidence: This is based on molecular characterization of the ZFY gene.

claim: The full-length variant of human ZFY has the ability to control transcription via transactivation.
source: Contrary to the short variant, the full-length variant has the ability to control transcription via transactivation (Decarpentrie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Decarpentrie et al., 2012.

claim: Zfy2 expresses the long isoform with higher transactivation activity compared to Zfy1.
source: This seems to be reflected in the mouse, as Zfy2 expresses the long isoform with higher transactivation activity compared to Zfy1 (Decarpentrie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Decarpentrie et al., 2012.

claim: Zfy genes are needed during pachynema for initiation and maintenance of MSCI, as well as apoptotic elimination of cells in which this process is defective.
source: It has been suggested that Zfy genes are needed during pachynema for initiation and maintenance of MSCI, as well as apoptotic elimination of cells in which this process is defective (Figures 3 and 4; Vernet et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vernet et al., 2016a and illustrated in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: During the first meiotic metaphase, Zfy2 regulates the SAC and is required to eliminate cells with unpaired sex chromosomes.
source: Later, during the first meiotic metaphase, Zfy2 regulates the SAC and is required to eliminate cells with unpaired sex chromosomes (Vernet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vernet et al., 2011.

claim: The addition of a Zfy2 transgene rescues the phenotype of univalent spermatocytes and ensures elimination of univalent spermatocytes.
source: The addition of a Zfy2 transgene rescues this phenotype and ensures elimination of univalent spermatocytes (Figure 4; Vernet et al., 2014; Vernet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vernet et al., 2014 and Vernet et al., 2011 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Zfy2, and to a lesser extent Zfy1, is required to promote completion of meiosis II.
source: Zfy2, and to a lesser extent Zfy1, is also required to promote completion of meiosis II, rescuing the meiotic block seen in Y-deletant models (Figure 4; Vernet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vernet et al., 2014 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Zfy2 is involved in spermatid morphogenesis, as transgenic integration of Zfy2 in Y-deletants improves spermatid morphology and increases the success rate of assisted reproduction.
source: Zfy2 is also involved in spermatid morphogenesis, as transgenic integration of Zfy2 in Y-deletants improves spermatid morphology and increases the success rate of assisted reproduction (Figure 4; Yamauchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamauchi et al., 2015 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Addition of Zfy2 contributes to the restructuring of the sperm head and development of the sperm tail.
source: Indeed, addition of Zfy2 contributes to the restructuring of the sperm head and development of the sperm tail (Figure 4; Vernet et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vernet et al., 2016b and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: The mouse Y long arm contains highly repetitive sequences and testis and murine-specific gene clusters consisting of three main gene families: Sycp3-like Y-linked (Sly), Spermiogenesis-specific transcript on the Y (Ssty) and Serine-rich Secreted Y-linked (Srsy).
source: The rest of the mouse Y euchromatin is encompassed within the long arm, which until 2014 remained mostly un-sequenced (Soh et al., 2014). The mouse Y long arm contains highly repetitive sequences and testis and murine-specific gene clusters consisting of three main gene families: Sycp3-like Y-linked (Sly), Spermiogenesis-specific transcript on the Y (Ssty) and Serine-rich Secreted Y-linked (Srsy) (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soh et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: Y deletant models with depletions of all three gene families (Sly, Ssty, and Srsy) show infertility and severe sperm abnormalities.
source: Y deletant models, which have depletions of all three gene families, show infertility and severe sperm abnormalities (Figure 4), associated with upregulation of spermatid-expressed sex chromosome genes (Conway et al., 1994; Ellis et al., 2005; Styrna et al., 1991; Touré et al., 2004; Yamauchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Conway et al., 1994; Ellis et al., 2005; Styrna et al., 1991; Touré et al., 2004; Yamauchi et al., 2010 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Knockdown of Sly causes subfertility and upregulation of spermatid genes.
source: Indeed, knockdown of Sly causes subfertility and upregulation of spermatid genes (Cocquet et al., 2009; Riel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cocquet et al., 2009 and Riel et al., 2013.

claim: When knockdown males were able to breed, SLY depletion was linked to female-biased litters.
source: When knockdown males were able to breed, SLY depletion was also linked to female-biased litters.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from knockdown studies.

claim: Knockdown of Slx/Slxl1 causes spermatid-specific sex-chromosome gene downregulation, as well as male-biased litters.
source: Conversely, knockdown of Slx/Slxl1, the X homologues to Sly, causes spermatid-specific sex-chromosome gene downregulation, as well as male-biased litters (Cocquet et al., 2012; Cocquet et al., 2010; Kruger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cocquet et al., 2012; Cocquet et al., 2010; Kruger et al., 2019.

claim: Sex-ratio skews likely result from differential fertilising abilities between X- and Y-bearing sperms in Sly and Slx/Slxl1 depleted models.
source: These sex-ratio skews likely result from differential fertilising abilities between X- and Y-bearing sperms in Sly and Slx/Slxl1 depleted models (Kruger et al., 2019; Rathje et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kruger et al., 2019 and Rathje et al., 2019.

claim: Knockdown of both X and Y families re-establishes correct sex ratio and transcriptional output.
source: Moreover, knockdown of both X and Y families re-establishes correct sex ratio and transcriptional output.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from knockdown studies.

claim: SLY and SLX/SLXL1 compete for chromatin occupancy at the loci of spermatid-expressed genes, especially on the sex chromosomes.
source: Mechanistically, SLY and SLX/SLXL1 compete for chromatin occupancy at the loci of spermatid-expressed genes, especially on the sex chromosomes (Moretti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moretti et al., 2020.

claim: SLY interacts with the histone-reader SSTY to recruit repressive transcriptional complexes, therefore modulating global spermatid-gene expression.
source: This is where SLY is thought to interact with the histone-reader SSTY to recruit repressive transcriptional complexes, therefore modulating global spermatid-gene expression (Comptour et al., 2014; Moretti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Comptour et al., 2014 and Moretti et al., 2020.

claim: The pressure to keep a balance in postmeiotic sex-chromosome expression and in sex ratio has created intragenomic conflict between sex chromosomes, with Sly and Slx/Slxl1 acting as antagonistic meiotic drivers.
source: Altogether, the pressure to keep a balance in postmeiotic sex-chromosome expression and in sex ratio has created intragenomic conflict between sex chromosomes, with Sly and Slx/Slxl1 acting as antagonistic meiotic drivers (see: Evolutionary forces and functional specialisation of the Y chromosome) (Cocquet et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2011; Larson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cocquet et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2011; Larson et al., 2018.

claim: Mice carrying only Sry, Eif2s3y, and Zfy can produce offspring through assisted reproduction, but they are infertile.
source: Although mice carrying only Sry, Eif2s3y, and Zfy can produce offspring through assisted reproduction, they are infertile.
evidence: This is based on experimental results discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Mice retaining most of the short arm, but no long arm, develop sperm with better morphology and have increased assisted-reproduction success compared to individuals expressing only Sry, Eif2s3y, and Zfy complements.
source: For instance, mice retaining most of the short arm, but no long arm, develop sperm with better morphology and have increased assisted-reproduction success compared to individuals expressing only Sry, Eif2s3y, and Zfy complements (Figure 4; Yamauchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yamauchi et al., 2015 and illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Transgenes usually integrate at random genomic locations, which can disturb expression of neighbouring genes.
source: Firstly, transgenes usually integrate at random genomic locations (Yan et al., 2013), which can disturb expression of neighbouring genes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yan et al., 2013.

claim: Transgenes often integrate in multiple copies and therefore have varying expression levels.
source: Furthermore, transgenes often integrate in multiple copies and therefore have varying expression levels (Mazeyrat et al., 2001; Royo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mazeyrat et al., 2001 and Royo et al., 2010.

claim: Targeting of Sry and Eif2s3y recapitulated the expected sex-reversed and spermatogonial-arrest phenotypes, respectively.
source: Targeting of the two most studied Y genes, Sry and Eif2s3y, recapitulated the expected sex-reversed and spermatogonial-arrest phenotypes, respectively (Kato et al., 2013; Matsubara et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2013; Zuo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kato et al., 2013; Matsubara et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2013; Zuo et al., 2017.

claim: Uty has partially-redundant functions with its X homologue Utx during embryonic development.
source: It was shown that this deeply conserved ancestral gene has partially-redundant functions with its X homologue Utx during embryonic development (Shpargel et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shpargel et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Following CRISPR/Cas9 editing, transcription through alternative start codons or skipping of mutated/deleted exons can allow functional protein formation.
source: However, we now know that following CRISPR/Cas9 editing, transcription through alternative start codons or skipping of mutated/deleted exons can allow functional protein formation (Lindeboom et al., 2016; Lindeboom et al., 2019 Sharpe and Cooper, 2017; Smits et al., 2019; Wiles, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lindeboom et al., 2016; Lindeboom et al., 2019; Sharpe and Cooper, 2017; Smits et al., 2019; Wiles, 2020.

claim: Non-conserved Y genes that are acquired within mammalian lineages tend to show testis-biased expression, and are therefore predicted to be linked to male fertility.
source: Although most Y-genes do not yet have ascribed functions, many could be important for spermatogenesis. Non-conserved Y genes that are acquired within mammalian lineages tend to show testis-biased expression, and are therefore predicted to be linked to male fertility (Bellott et al., 2014; Godfrey et al., 2020; Mitchell, 2000; Soh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bellott et al., 2014; Godfrey et al., 2020; Mitchell, 2000; Soh et al., 2014.

claim: Teyorf1, Prssly and H2al2 were discovered only recently, and their functions in fertility have not been investigated.
source: In the case of the mouse, Testis expressed, Chromosome Y open reading frame 1 (Teyorf1), Protease, serine-like, Y (Prssly) and H2A histone family member L2 (H2al2) (Soh et al., 2014; Figure 2 and Table 2) were discovered only recently, and their functions in fertility have therefore not been investigated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soh et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: Some ancestral genes seem to have functionally diverged from their X-homologues.
source: Interestingly, some of these ancestral genes seem to have functionally diverged from their X-homologues (Bellott et al., 2014; Snell and Turner, 2018) and evolved testis-biased expression, suggesting a specialised role in spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bellott et al., 2014 and Snell and Turner, 2018.

claim: Deletions encompassing DDX3Y and USP9Y have been recorded in sub-fertile men.
source: Furthermore, deletions encompassing DDX3Y and USP9Y have been recorded in sub-fertile men (Sun et al., 1999; Vogt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sun et al., 1999 and Vogt et al., 2008.

claim: Divergence between Y and X chromosome regulatory regions can lead to expression, and potentially phenotypic differences between XY and XX individuals.
source: Divergence between Y and X chromosome regulatory regions can lead to expression, and potentially phenotypic differences between XY and XX individuals (Godfrey et al., 2020; Naqvi et al., 2019; Naqvi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Godfrey et al., 2020; Naqvi et al., 2019; Naqvi et al., 2018.

claim: The human Y chromosome is roughly 60% heterochromatic.
source: Whereas the human Y chromosome is roughly 60 % heterochromatic, the mouse Y chromosome is 99.9% euchromatic (Skaletsky et al., 2003; Soh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Skaletsky et al., 2003 and Soh et al., 2014.

claim: The mouse Y chromosome is 99.9% euchromatic.
source: Whereas the human Y chromosome is roughly 60 % heterochromatic, the mouse Y chromosome is 99.9% euchromatic (Skaletsky et al., 2003; Soh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Skaletsky et al., 2003 and Soh et al., 2014.

claim: The human Y shares seven ancestral protein-coding genes with the murine Y.
source: The human Y shares seven ancestral protein-coding genes with the murine Y (labelled).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 where genes are labeled.
